text: Radiation transport and moment methods Radiation transport resolves intensity in space, direction and frequency. Moment methods reduce the angular dimension but require closure for information removed by integration. Problem and representative equations Use frequency-integrated grey intensity I in a static medium, with isotropic emissivity η and absorption coefficient κ of inverse-length units; omit scattering here. Define E=(1/c)∫I dΩ, F=∫nI dΩ and P=(1/c)∫nnI dΩ. Moment equations for E and F require a prescription for P. 1c∂tI+n⋅∇I=η−κI,∂tE+∇⋅F=4πη−cκE,c−2∂tF+∇⋅P=−κF/c.c1​∂t​I+n⋅∇I=η−κI,∂t​E+∇⋅F=4πη−cκE,c−2∂t​F+∇⋅P=−κF/c. Grey (gray) approximation A grey (gray) model uses frequency-integrated intensity without resolving frequency. This is a separate choice from the treatment of angle: the grey approximation is not itself a diffusion approximation or an M1 closure. The existing grey transport and M1 examples are limited to a static medium and fixed inputs. Compare the angular-transport and M1 releases below within their own conditions. They do not establish general accuracy of the grey approximation against frequency-resolved calculations. Grey angular transport: the fixed Su–Olson1997 example · Grey angular transport and M1: the 2D absorber shadow Radiation diffusion approximation The radiation diffusion approximation relates the radiation flux to the gradient of energy density in an optically thick, nearly isotropic regime. Its role differs from the grey approximation, which integrates over frequency. The existing Su–Olson1996 example advances diffusion equations with non-equilibrium radiation–matter exchange. The Su–Olson1997 angular-transport release also contains fixed diffusion-limit controls in a separate periodic setting. The coordinate normalizations, boundaries and references of these problems are not identical. These examples do not establish fixed-grid asymptotic preservation (AP) or diffusion-approximation accuracy under arbitrary conditions. Flux-limited diffusion (FLD) is a separate closure with a flux limiter. The atlas explains it but does not yet provide a dedicated nonlinear FLD solver and validation example. The diffusion and M1 examples above are not counted as FLD implementations. Non-equilibrium diffusion: the fixed Su–Olson1996 example · Angular transport and fixed diffusion-limit controls Algorithm Discrete ordinates discretizes angle directly; moment methods close P=D E. M1 obtains D locally from E and F, while flux-limited diffusion instead approximates F from the gradient of E. Check optically thick and free-streaming limits and couple matter exchange through a consistent energy balance. Conditions and pitfalls M1 generally cannot propagate crossing beams independently. FLD ties flux to the energy gradient, limiting shadows and strongly anisotropic fields. A reduced light speed changes transport/relaxation scales and must be justified against the physical time scales of interest. The two historical companions (pure absorption and space/angle convergence) solve μ∂xI=−κI in a one-dimensional steady purely absorbing slab with specified inflow. Those two releases do not validate general radiation moment closures, scattering, time dependence, multiple frequencies or fluid coupling. Consult the separate releases above for the scope of later grey transport, diffusion and M1 examples. What to check Test exponential absorption, isotropic diffusion, free streaming/shadows and crossing beams separately. Check E≥0, |F|≤cE, matter-plus-radiation energy and angular/spatial/time convergence. Distinguish closure error from discretization error. Use directional Beer–Lambert solutions and a continuum-angle exponential integral, separating upwind spatial error at fixed ordinates from angular-quadrature error with exact ray propagation. Check inflow–outflow versus volume absorption and positivity separately; a balance check alone does not establish angular-distribution accuracy. At optical depths 0.1/0.7/3, cross-check the continuum-angle reference using expn and a separate adaptive QUADPACK quadrature. Independent transport sampling draws μ=√U for the incident flux and counts transmission as a Bernoulli variable. Check binomial intervals and RMSE over 64 finite-sample replicates; nominal 95% coverage is not claimed for arbitrary inputs or samples. Check fixed inputs: separate scoped releases Check each example’s inputs, observables, diagnostic definitions and scope. What a passing check establishes depends on its acceptance criteria and differs from a general mathematical guarantee. Historical inputs, measurements and criteria are preserved. Discrete-ordinate radiation transport through an absorbing slab Computation for a fixed target Discretize steady pure-absorption transfer in angle and space, checking Beer–Lambert rays and integrated exit flux. Multiple scattering, thermal emission, frequency redistribution, moving media and radiation–fluid coupling are unimplemented. This does not reproduce full DISORT functionality/stabilization.
